name: SN65HVD230DR
title: SN65HVD230, SN65HVD231, SN65HVD232: 3.3 V CAN bus transceivers, SOIC-8
summary: A family of three CAN physical-layer transceivers that run from a single 3.3 V supply and meet ISO 11898 signalling at up to 1 Mbps. Each turns the single-ended transmit and receive lines of a CAN controller into the differential CANH/CANL pair. The SN65HVD230 adds a low-current standby state in which only the receiver stays alive (370 µA typ); the SN65HVD231 adds a sleep state that turns both driver and receiver off (40 nA typ); both use pin 8 (RS) for high-speed, slope-control or low-power selection and pin 5 for a VCC/2 reference. The SN65HVD232 has neither feature, with pins 5 and 8 unconnected. Bus pins withstand 16 kV HBM, tolerate common-mode voltages from -2 V to 7 V and stay high impedance when the node is unpowered.

circuits.title: 3.3 V and 5 V CAN transceiver system
circuits.description: Three nodes share one twisted-pair bus. Two of them use 5 V SN65HVD251 transceivers and one uses the 3.3 V SN65HVD230; each transceiver's D and R go to the CANTX and CANRX pins of its own DSP (TMS320LF243 on the 5 V nodes, TMS320LF2407A on the 3.3 V node). Every transceiver has 0.1 µF from VCC to GND and its RS pin grounded, which selects high-speed mode; Vref is left unconnected. A 120 Ω resistor across CANH and CANL at each end of the bus terminates it.

notes: Bus lines are 40 m at most and each stub from the bus to a transceiver 0.3 m at most.
Each DSP also connects to sensor, actuator or control equipment.

circuits.title: RS driven by a DSP output for high-speed and standby operation
circuits.description: A general-purpose output of the DSP (IOPF6) drives RS directly. Holding it below 1 V runs the transceiver in high-speed mode; raising it above 0.75 VCC puts the SN65HVD230 into listen-only standby.

circuits.title: Slope control and standby from a DSP output
circuits.description: A resistor of 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ sits between RS and the DSP output IOPF6. With the output low the resistor sets the driver's edge rate, about 15 V/µs at 10 kΩ and about 2 V/µs at 100 kΩ; with the output high the SN65HVD230 enters standby whatever the resistor.

operation.text: The three parts are the physical layer between a 3.3 V CAN controller (the TMS320Lx240x DSPs are the named example) and an ISO 11898 bus at up to 1 Mbps. The driver gives a differential output to the bus and the receiver gives a logic output back to the controller. They are pin compatible with each other, so one board layout takes any of them, though they do not behave identically. The footprint matches the PCA82C250, which they replace at lower power.

D low drives CANH high and CANL low: a dominant bus with about 2 V between the lines. D high or open leaves both outputs high impedance and the termination resistors pull the bus recessive, both lines near 2.3 V. The receiver output R goes low when VID reaches 0.9 V, high when VID is 0.5 V or less, and is undefined between. Open bus inputs give R high.

The bus operates over -2 V to 7 V common mode and withstands ±25 V common-mode transients. The devices have cross-wire, loss-of-ground, overvoltage and overtemperature protection. In thermal shutdown, whether from high ambient temperature or excess output current, the bus pins turn high impedance and D and R go to logic high. Bus pins carry 16 kV HBM; all pins 4 kV HBM and 1 kV CDM. The receiver is fail-safe: open bus wires give a high output.

While VCC is low the bus pins are held high impedance, so power-up and power-down cause no bus glitch and a board can be hot-plugged. A node with no power leaves the bus undisturbed. Transceivers lacking this have a low output impedance when off, so an unpowered one draws heavy current and can upset the whole network. The high bus input impedance lets up to 120 nodes share one bus.

On the SN65HVD230 and SN65HVD231, RS (pin 8) held below 1 V gives high-speed mode: the output transistors switch as fast as they can with no limit on edge rate. Cable length and radiated emissions are its only constraints, both of which slope control addresses. In this mode RS sources up to 450 µA. A DSP output can drive RS directly to switch between high speed (below 1 V) and standby (above 0.75 VCC).

Fitting a resistor between RS and ground (or a logic-low output) slows the driver edges to reduce interference on unshielded cable. The edge rate is proportional to the current out of RS: 10 kΩ gives about 15 V/µs and 100 kΩ about 2 V/µs. Slower edges lengthen the loop delay (about 100 ns at 10 kΩ, about 500 ns at 100 kΩ), which shortens the longest bus that still meets CAN bit timing; shielded cable is the other way to cut emissions.

RS above 0.75 VCC switches off the driver and leaves the receiver running at 370 µA typ, so the node only listens and is passive to the bus, with or without a slope resistor fitted. A dominant bus (VID above about 900 mV) still shows at R; the controller sees the activity and returns RS below 1.2 V to re-enable the driver, which takes 0.55 µs typ, 1.5 µs max.

If a faulty CAN controller sends continuously and holds the bus, the host can raise RS on the SN65HVD230 to drop into standby; the driver outputs go high impedance and free the bus, even if the controller itself has stopped responding.

RS high turns off both driver and receiver; supply current falls to 0.04 µA typ, 1 µA max. The bus pins are high impedance and D and R default to logic high. The part stays asleep until RS is taken low, and wakes in 3 µs typ, 5 µs max.
The basic transceiver with no low-power mode, no slope control and no reference output; pins 5 and 8 are not connected.
Pin 5 of the SN65HVD230 and SN65HVD231 gives a VCC/2 reference: 0.45 VCC to 0.55 VCC for loads within ±5 µA, 0.4 VCC to 0.6 VCC within ±50 µA.
Loop delay is the driver delay from D to the bus plus the receiver delay from the bus to R. Through the SN65HVD230 with RS = 0 it measures 70.7 ns. Typical bus cable delays a signal by about 5 ns/m.

D takes the controller's transmit output and R feeds its receive input; CANH and CANL go to the bus. The bus is normally a twisted pair of 120 Ω characteristic impedance in a half-duplex multidrop arrangement, with a 120 Ω resistor at each end to suppress reflections. In the mixed 3.3 V / 5 V example the bus runs to 40 m with stubs of 0.3 m at most.

In the dominant state the SN65HVD230's differential output lies between 1.5 V and 3 V into 60 Ω, the same limits ISO 11898 sets and 5 V transceivers meet; the recessive level is set by the terminations, not the driver. The receivers switch at 500 mV and 900 mV over -2 V to 7 V common mode, as 5 V receivers do. The one difference is a dominant common-mode level a few hundred millivolts below a 5 V driver's, which is not fully to ISO 11898 but is rejected by differential receivers without effect on data, noise margin or error rate. Electrical compatibility alone does not guarantee interchangeability; that needs equipment testing.

Each bus input has 110 kΩ to VCC and a 45 kΩ / 9 kΩ divider into the receiver with 9 kΩ to VCC, clamped by a 16 V device to VCC and a 20 V device to ground. The bus outputs are clamped by 16 V to VCC and 20 V to ground. The D input has a 100 kΩ pull-up to VCC behind a 1 kΩ series resistor with 9 V clamps. R drives out through 5 Ω with a 9 V clamp to ground.
The devices have limited built-in ESD protection; during storage or handling their leads are shorted together or they are kept in conductive foam.
